title: Love grows with knowing (10:6)
hookLine: one loves God according to how much one knows
tomorrow: so what would a plan of return look like on paper?

cards: A song you skipped the first time can become the one you play on repeat, once you learn the words, catch the bass line under the chorus, find out who it was written for. Can you love what you barely know?
Maimonides says not much, and he means it as good news.

teach.h: ACCORDING TO THE KNOWING, THE LOVE.
teach.b: Here's his line from chapter ten. A person loves the Holy One only by the knowledge with which they know Him.

According to the knowing, the love: if little, then little; if much, then much. So, he says, a person should give themselves to understanding the wisdoms that make their Creator known to them, as far as a human can.
They expect love and learning to sit at opposite ends: the heart over here, the head over there. Maimonides fuses them.
In the very first pages of his law book he says the same: look closely at the world's wonders, and love wakes up. Learning isn't the cold part of faith. It's the fuel.

Try it with the senses. A pharmacist can look at a pill most of us couldn't name and tell you what it does, who it helps, what it must never be taken with. A gardener knows a plant by the smell of a crushed leaf.
Knowing something that closely isn't cold.
It's a kind of care. One honest note: other Jewish teachers, later on, put more weight on the heart's simple devotion, open to the unlearned as much as the scholar.
Maimonides stands at the knowing end of that conversation, and the tradition keeps both voices.

how: Torah study is a central Jewish practice, and some learn a set portion each day; Maimonides' 10:6 is often quoted for why study and love belong together.

games.q: what does “love grows with knowing” mean?
o: the more you love, the less you need to know
love of God needs no learning, only feeling
the more you know God, the more you can love

p: knowing a pill as a kind of care
learning as the fuel of love

s: for Maimonides, love and learning pull in opposite directions
he fuses them: according to the knowing, the love.
he says to give yourself to the wisdoms that make the Creator known
as far as a human can.
every Jewish teacher puts knowing first, as Maimonides does
later teachers put more weight on the heart's simple devotion. the tradition keeps both.

games.q: your friend says she'd love Shabbat more if it weren't 'just a bunch of rules.' what would Maimonides suggest?
o: learn why each piece is there; love grows with knowing.
skip the learning and wait for the feeling to arrive.
keep the rules without asking; asking weakens love.
games.why: for Maimonides, the love follows the knowing. learning what a thing is for is how it becomes lovable.

practice: Pick up one small thing near you: a leaf, a coin, your own hand. For the whole sit, learn it: its edges, its weight, its temperature, one detail you've never noticed before. Let the looking get slower and closer.

wordCard.voice: Love grows with knowing: Maimonides' rule. Know a little, love a little; know more, love more.

orig.note: Hebrew: knowledge. In 10:6, the love follows the knowing.

carryVoice: Something to keep: love grows with knowing, and learning is the fuel, not the cold part. Twenty-eight down.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 10:6 (one loves the Holy One only by the knowledge with which one knows Him; according to the knowing, the love; devote yourself to the wisdoms that make the Creator known)
Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah (Yesodei ha-Torah) 2:2 (contemplating creation brings love)
